# Introduction

This section of the module will introduce you to the foundations of biological data analysis using programming language R. You will learn how to work with single-cell RNA sequencing data to identify distinct cell types within complex tissues, and how to determine which cell types are associated with specific diseases through enrichment analysis.

Through practical, hands-on sessions, you will gain experience with key computational tools and workflows used in modern biology. These skills will help you develop an intuition for analysing large-scale biological datasets and extracting meaningful insights from gene expression patterns across different cell types.


## Tutorial Overview

**Day 1:** scRNA-Seq Analysis Basics - From Raw Data To Cell Types  
**Day 2:** EWCE R Package - Cell Type Enrichment Analysis


# R Kickstart (Required)

We’ll be working with R, a programming language designed for data analysis and
statistics. It is recommended that you familiarise yourself with the basics of R
programming before the session. There are many free resources online to get you
started.

Here are some recommendations (click on the titles to launch). Please go through
at least one of them if you are unfamiliar with R.

- [**Youtube: R Programming for ABSOLUTE beginners**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FY8BISK5DpM)  
  [*14 minutes!*]  
  A short intro to R programming covering the basic, creating and using
  variables.

- [**Youtube: R Programming Tutorial**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_V8eKsto3Ug)  
  [*1-2 hours*]  
  A very gentle introduction to R, which also includes instructions for
  installing R and RStudio.
  
  You may skip the last few sections on clustering and principal components
  for now.

- [**Swirl**](https://swirlstats.com/)  
  [*A few hours*]  
  An interactive R programming course that runs within RStudio itself. You can
  learn the basics of R programming while writing R code.

- [**R for Data Science**](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/)  
  [*A few hours*]  
  A free online book that
  covers the basics of R programming and data analysis using the tidyverse
  packages.
  
  Bite-sized chapters with very simple language. Highly recommended for
  beginners.

Feel free to ask any doubts you may have during the session!

# Software Requirements

Please make sure you have the following installed on your system before the
session.

### 1. R (version 4.5)

The workshop materials were tested with **R 4.5.1**.
R 4.6 has not yet been tested by the workshop team; if you already have R 4.6,
run the check below and tell us the result.

##### Download Links
```
Windows: https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/
MacOS: https://cloud.r-project.org > MacOS
```

### 2. RStudio Desktop
RStudio Desktop is the program we will be using for writing and executing R
code. Such tools are known as Integrated Development Environments (IDEs).
Another popular example of an IDE is [VSCode](https://code.visualstudio.com/).

```
Download: https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
```

### 3. R packages
Within the RStudio console, run the installation code below. It is the same
code as `install-packages.R` in the setup folder that came with this document,
so you can instead open that file in RStudio (*File > Open File*) and click
**Source** at the top right of the editor.

![R Studio Console](assets/preamble/rstudio-console.jpg){width=80%}

The console is where we will be executing all the R code. Sometimes, you may
have two panes on the left side of RStudio. In such cases, the console is
usually the bottom-left pane.

(Copying and pasting ONE BLOCK AT A TIME is fine.)

**Errors and warnings are different.** An *error* stops a command; a *warning*
is a message that may or may not matter. Do not assume an installation worked:
the check in step 4 tells you. If an installation reports an error, or asks a
question you are unsure how to answer, copy the message (or take a screenshot)
and email it to any of the tutors before going further.

**What to expect.** The first block downloads R packages from CRAN and
Bioconductor: several hundred MB, mostly Seurat and the packages it needs.
On a slow connection or an older laptop this can take a long time. Leave it
running, and do not close RStudio while it works. Lots of red text scrolling
past is normal: R prints its progress messages in red.

```{R, eval = FALSE}
# Install up to 8 packages at once, and allow slow downloads up to 20 minutes
options(Ncpus = 8, timeout = max(1200, getOption("timeout")))

# Bioconductor's installer (Bioconductor hosts many bioinformatics packages)
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}

# Workshop packages. update = FALSE leaves packages you already have alone.
BiocManager::install(
  c("Seurat", "EWCE", "ewceData", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "ggdendro"),
  update = FALSE, ask = FALSE
)
```

If R asks *"Update all/some/none? [a/s/n]"*, type `n` and press Enter.

Next, load the two main packages. This shows whether the installation really
worked.

```{R, eval = FALSE}
library(Seurat)
library(EWCE)
```

If either line says *there is no package called 'X'*, a package that Seurat
or EWCE needs did not install (in 2026 this was often `KEGGREST`). Install
that package on its own, replacing `X` with the name in the message, then run
the two `library()` lines again:

```{R, eval = FALSE}
BiocManager::install("X", update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)
```

Finally, download the Day 2 example data (about 100 MB) so there is no wait
during the session.

```{R, eval = FALSE}
# The data are kept in a folder on your computer (a "cache"). This line lets
# R create that folder without asking first.
ExperimentHub::setExperimentHubOption("ASK", FALSE)

invisible(ewceData::ctd())
invisible(ewceData::example_genelist())
```

If R asks *"... does not exist, create directory? (yes/no)"*, type `yes` and
press Enter.

You do not need to download the Day 1 data now: the Day 1 worksheet
downloads it (7.6 MB) when you reach that step.

### 4. Check that everything works

Open `check-setup.R` from the same setup folder in RStudio (*File > Open
File*) and click **Source** at the top right of the editor. The results appear
in the console. Every line should say `PASS`.

If a line says `FAIL`, email that line and the message below it to any of the
tutors. If the problem cannot be fixed before the session, you can
still take part by working with a partner and using the prepared outputs.


# Contact

**Before the workshop:** email any of the tutors. Include the error message (or
a screenshot) and the output of `check-setup.R`.

**During the workshop:** ask any tutor in the session.
